_comment: AI-FACING UC2 MONITORING TOOLS — the read side of the hook execution model.
These ARE real MCP tools (is_tool=1, is_hook=0), unlike the runtime hooks in
helpers-hooks-user-directives.json which the AI writes calls to but never
invokes. The user's generated runner records what happened through
aimfp.hooks while no session is open; these are how the AI sees it after.
They are also where the rewritten user_directive_monitor workflow maps its
steps. Note there is deliberately NO process inspection: a dead runner is
detected by next_scheduled_time falling into the past, which is why the
original workflow's PID and APScheduler checks were removed rather than

helpers.name: get_directive_execution_stats

parameters.name: directive_id
parameters.description: One directive, or omit for all

parameters.name: project_root
parameters.description: Project root; defaults to the session root

helpers.purpose: Read execution statistics from directive_executions joined to directive names and statuses, for one user directive or all of them. Includes a derived error_rate per row. This is how the AI sees what the user's automation did while no session was open — executions, successes, errors, average and maximum duration, and the last recorded error.
helpers.error_handling: Returns success=False with an explanatory error when user_directives.db is absent (a Use Case 1 project has no user directives). Directives that have never run still appear, with zero counts, via a LEFT JOIN.
return_statements: A high error_rate or a stale last_execution_time is worth raising with the user — the runner fires without an AI session, so nobody has seen these numbers.
For the errors behind a count, call get_recent_directive_errors: the database keeps only the LAST error per directive, while the JSONL log keeps 90 days of history.
For an overall verdict rather than raw numbers, call check_directive_health.

helpers.name: get_recent_directive_errors

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Maximum records to return, newest first

parameters.name: directive_id
parameters.description: Filter to one directive, or omit for all

parameters.name: project_root
parameters.description: Project root; defaults to the session root

helpers.purpose: Tail the JSON-lines directive error log, newest first, optionally filtered to one directive. Each record carries directive_id, error_type, message, timestamp, and a full traceback when the failure came from a handler exception. The database keeps only the last error per directive (store_last_error_only defaults to 1), so this file is the only place error history survives.
helpers.error_handling: Returns success=False when user_directives.db is absent or limit < 1. A missing log file is an empty read rather than an error — a project whose directives have never failed has no error log, which is the good case. Unparseable records are counted in malformed_lines rather than hidden; a truncated final line is normal when a run was interrupted mid-write.
return_statements: A repeated error_type across records points at a systemic cause — a dead dependency or a changed credential — rather than a flaky run.
error_type 'handler_exception' means the user's own handler raised and carries a traceback; 'execution_error' means the runner reported failure itself without one.
A non-zero malformed_lines is usually a run interrupted mid-write. Many malformed lines suggest something other than AIMFP is writing to this log.

helpers.name: check_directive_health

parameters.name: project_root
parameters.description: Project root; defaults to the session root

parameters.name: error_rate_threshold
parameters.description: Error rate at or above which a directive is reported degraded

helpers.purpose: Assess every user directive and report which need attention. Health states, in the precedence applied: 'error' (the directive's own status is error), 'overdue' (next_scheduled_time is in the past — the runner said when it would next fire and did not), 'degraded' (error rate at or above threshold), 'never_run' (active but never executed, so the runner may not be deployed), or 'ok'. Returns a per-directive verdict with a one-line explanation plus a summary count per state, designed to render as a single sentence at session start.
helpers.error_handling: Returns success=False with an explanatory error when user_directives.db is absent. Classification itself is a pure function of the rows, the current time, and the threshold.
return_statements: If needs_attention is true, tell the user which directives and why before continuing with other work — these ran unattended and nobody has seen the outcome.
'overdue' is the dead-runner signal: the directive's own scheduler declared a next run time and that moment has passed. Check that the generated runner is still deployed and running.
'never_run' on an active directive usually means implementation completed but the runner was never deployed or its scheduler was never registered.
A directive with no next_scheduled_time can never be reported overdue. If its runner does not call set_next_scheduled_time when scheduling, silence is indistinguishable from health.
